property_summary: Any call to lockInGuess that does not send exactly 1 ether must revert (so reverted == (amount != 1 ether)).

In the original contract, lockInGuess only succeeds (does not revert) when exactly 1 ether is sent; in the mutant it can succeed with other amounts, so the test asserts that success implies the sent value equals 1 ether.
Whenever lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert), the contract's balance increases by exactly 1 ether as a result of that call.

property_summary: If lockInGuess call does not revert then the value sent with that call was exactly 1 ether (i.e., non-reverting implies amount == 1 ether).

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, if the caller sends exactly 1 ether when calling lockInGuess(...) then the reference contract always records the guess (guesses[msg.sender].block != 0) while the mutant that removed the msg.value check can be invoked with a different value and thus be called with non-1-ether payments that still record the guess (so the general rule: only calls that pay exactly 1 ether cause the guess to be recorded in the reference; the mutant allows guesses to be recorded with other payment amounts and thus violates this restriction).

For any caller and any calldata, the reference contract only accepts lockInGuess when msg.value == 1 ether (call succeeds and records a nonzero block); the mutant that removed the msg.value require allows calls with other msg.value to succeed and record state, violating that restriction.

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert) if and only if the caller sends exactly 1 ether to the reference contract; the mutant removed that require so it may accept calls with other ether amounts — the test fuzzes the sent amount and actor and asserts that only sending exactly 1 ether yields a successful call on the reference, a property the mutant can violate.

Invariant: After any single call to lockInGuess(hash) from any address sending any ether amount, the reference C records guesses[msg.sender].block != 0 if and only if the call sent exactly 1 ether; the mutant (which removed the msg.value require) can record a guess when sent a different amount — we fuzz sender and amount to find such a case.

For the reference C, any call to lockInGuess that sends a non-zero ether amount but not exactly 1 ether will revert (so only exactly 1 ether payments can succeed); the mutant removed the msg.value==1 ether require and therefore allows some non-1-ether calls to succeed, violating this rule.

After a successful lockInGuess call, the stored Guess.block for the caller is always strictly greater than the current block.number at the time of the call's completion in the reference contract (it sets block.number+1), but the mutant that stores block.number can make Guess.block equal to the current block, violating that rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether, the stored guesses(caller).block in the correct contract is strictly greater than the block number at the time of the call (block.number at end of the call), while the mutant that stores block.number can make it equal — so the invariant 'guesses(caller).block > block.number at call completion' holds for the reference and is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the stored guesses(caller).block is strictly greater than the block number at the time of that call's completion; the mutant that writes block.number can make it equal and thus violate this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the stored guesses(caller).block is never less than the block.number at the time of call completion (reference sets it to block.number+1 so stored block >= currentBlock+1), whereas the mutant that writes block.number can make the stored block equal to the current block causing stored block < block.number+1 — we assert stored block != block.number to distinguish them.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying 1 ether, the reference contract always sets guesses(caller).block to a strictly positive value that is strictly greater than the block number at which the NEXT call to settle would compare (i.e., the stored block is in the future relative to the block when lockInGuess completed) — equivalently, immediately after lockInGuess returns in the reference, a subsequent call to settle in the same block MUST NOT be able to read a stored guess.block equal to the current block and therefore the reference guarantees that settle called in the same block cannot succeed; the mutant that writes block.number can set guess.block to the current block and thus allows settle to see guess.block == block.number and potentially behave differently (fail the guard block.number > guesses[msg.sender].block), so we assert that calling settle immediately after lockInGuess in the same block always reverts (reference) but the mutant sometimes allows it to proceed (i.e., does not revert).

For any caller and guess hash, immediately after a successful lockInGuess(call) the stored guess and block are set such that the stored guess equals the provided hash; the mutant that swaps the two assignments can transiently make the stored guess appear unset to external observers that read the struct in the same transaction ordering (i.e. the mapping entry's guess must equal the supplied hash after lockInGuess), which the mutant can violate for some interleavings observed by a caller reading state via the contract's public surface.

After any successful lockInGuess by an address sending 1 ether, the contract's public getter for that address's stored guess (the auto-generated mapping getter) must equal the provided hash; the mutant that swaps assignments can for some inputs cause the stored guess getter to not equal the supplied hash immediately after the call.

For any caller who funds and calls lockInGuess with 1 ether, immediately after the call the contract's public mapping getter returns a nonzero block number for that caller (guesses(caller).block != 0); the mutant swapping assignments can transiently leave guess zero/unchanged in some interleavings, violating this observable invariant for some inputs.

For any caller that funds the contract with exactly 1 ether and calls lockInGuess(hash) in a single transaction, the reference contract always records the provided guess hash in guesses(caller).guess (the public getter) after the call returns; the mutant that swaps the assignments can, for some block-number value fuzzed in together with the caller, cause the recorded guess to be different (transiently unset) and thus violate this rule.

For any caller X who sends exactly 1 ether and calls lockInGuess(hash) in one transaction, after the call returns the contract's public mapping getter guesses(X).block must be nonzero and guesses(X).guess must equal the provided hash; the mutant that swaps the two assignments can in some execution interleave cause the public getter to temporarily expose guesses(X).guess as zero when read in the same transaction via an external call (here simulated by a helper that calls back into C to read the getter), breaking that observable rule.

For any caller address and valid 1 ether payment, the reference contract always accepts lockInGuess (call succeeds) as long as the caller has no existing lock; the mutant rejects calls when msg.sender == address(0) (which can occur when a contract forwards a call using DELEGATECALL-like scenarios are not possible from EOAs, but we can simulate a call from the zero address by having an intermediate contract perform a CALL with from==address(0) via a selfdestruct-funded proxy pattern) — thus there exist inputs where reference accepts but mutant rejects.

For any caller address and 1 ether payment, the reference C always allows lockInGuess to succeed when the caller has no existing guess; the mutant additionally rejects calls that originate from the zero address, so there exist inputs (a call originating from address(0)) where the reference accepts but the mutant reverts.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, the reference contract accepts a first lockInGuess call (succeeds when paying 1 ether and no prior guess), but the mutant additionally rejects calls that originate from address(0); the property asserts that a lockInGuess forwarded through a helper that forwards the call preserving msg.sender succeeds for all non-zero forwarded senders, and the mutant will fail for a crafted helper that makes the call originate from address(0).

For any nonzero caller that pays exactly 1 ether and has no existing guess, lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert); the mutant additionally rejects calls that originate from address(0), so a call that genuinely originates from address(0) will succeed on the reference but revert on the mutant.

For any caller address A (including contracts) that pays exactly 1 ether and has no existing guess, calling lockInGuess from A always succeeds on the reference C; the mutant rejects calls that genuinely originate from address(0) (i.e. a call where msg.sender == address(0)), so there exists an adversarial helper that can cause a call whose msg.sender is address(0) and thus the mutant reverts while the reference accepts it.

For any caller who locked a correct winning guess and is a contract whose fallback/receive reverts, the reference (using transfer) always reverts the payout call so settle() overall still succeeds (because transfer bubbles revert) — actually transfer forwards 2300 gas and will revert if the recipient reverts; the mutant using call will propagate the callee revert as a failed call causing require(success) and thus can cause settle() to revert for some adversarial contract; we assert that for all fuzzed inputs the reference's settle() call DOES NOT revert when the caller is a normal EOA winner but DOES revert for at least some adversarial contract winner, so the mutant's behavior differs (the test deploys a reverting recipient to trigger the difference).

For any admissible fuzzed guess and attacker address, when a player locks a winning guess and is a reverting contract, the reference contract C (which uses transfer) will still allow settle() to succeed (transfer will revert the payout but because transfer forwards only 2300 gas it will cause the payout to revert and thus the reference behavior ensures contract state is reset and settle() does not propagate a different observable failure), whereas the mutated version using call may cause settle() to revert due to require(success) failing when the recipient reverts; the test asserts that calling settle() on the reference does not revert (ok == true) for all admissible inputs while the mutant will fail for some input (the adversarial reverting recipient) — we construct a reverting helper and fuzz the guess bytes32 and an arbitrary uint to be wide.

For every admissible winning scenario where a player locked a guess and then calls settle, the reference contract's settle call always returns (does not revert) even if the recipient's fallback reverts because transfer bubbles; the mutant using call{value:...} plus require(success) can revert when the recipient reverts, so there exist inputs (a reverting recipient) that make the mutant's settle revert while the reference's settle does not.

For any actor who locked a guess and later calls settle, the reference C's settle() always completes (does not revert) even when the recipient contract's fallback reverts because transfer either succeeds or reverts safely, whereas the mutated version using call{value:...} plus require(success) can cause settle() to revert for some recipient contracts that revert on receive/fallback.

For any caller/address that locked a correct winning guess and then calls settle(), the reference contract C (which uses transfer) will always allow settle() to return (ok == true) when the recipient is a normal EOA or a contract whose receive/fallback DOES NOT consume excessive gas, whereas the mutant using call with require(success) can revert when the recipient's fallback deliberately reverts; thus the reference always succeeds for all admissible inputs while the mutant fails for some adversarial recipient contracts.

After a successful settle call, the reference contract always clears the stored guess.block for the caller (making future settle calls revert with block==0), whereas the mutant leaves it set so a second settle can proceed (or behave differently); the test fuzzes an attacker address and a target block offset to witness this difference.

After a successful settle call by any player, the reference implementation always clears that player's stored guess.block to 0 (so a subsequent settle immediately reverts because block==0), while the mutant leaves guess.block non-zero allowing a second settle attempt to proceed (or not revert) for some inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess, calling settle in the reference reverts if called in the same block as the lock (i.e. settle requires current block > stored block), whereas the mutant allowing >= permits settle to proceed in the same block and thus can pay out or succeed when the reference would still reject.

For any caller who locked a guess, calling settle in the same block as lockInGuess always reverts (reference requires block.number > stored block), whereas the mutant allowing >= lets settle proceed in that same block (breaking the rule).

For every caller who lockInGuess with a target block = block.number+1, the reference contract disallows calling settle in the same block as the stored block (i.e. settle must revert when called at block == stored block), while the mutant allows settle to proceed (not revert) when block.number == stored block — so the property is: calling settle in the stored block always reverts on the reference but may succeed on the mutant.

For any address that locked a guess, calling settle in the SAME block as lockInGuess always leaves the contract balance unchanged (reference reverts and thus no transfer); the mutant allowing >= can execute settle in that same block and may transfer funds causing address(c).balance to decrease for some inputs.

For any address and guess, calling settle in the same block as the stored target block always reverts on the reference (so the call does not succeed), while the mutant (using >=) allows settle to succeed for some inputs in that same block, breaking that invariant.

For any address that locked a guess equal to keccak256(blockhash(b)) where b is the stored target block, calling settle in the correct contract will only pay out if the stored block's blockhash matches the guess (i.e., payout depends on the stored block's blockhash), whereas the mutant computes the answer from the current blockhash and can wrongly pay out (or fail to pay) for inputs where block.number's blockhash differs from the stored block's blockhash.
